name: Market Socialism
summary: Market socialism holds that the means of production should be socially owned, by the public or by the workers who use them, while goods, services and usually capital goods are exchanged in competitive markets. Its theorists reject both capitalist ownership, with its unearned property income and concentrated wealth, and Soviet-style central planning, which they regard as inefficient and authoritarian. Most modern designs pair self-managed or publicly owned firms with public banks or public control over new investment, and aim at greater equality, workplace democracy and political democracy.
scope: The theoretical family as defined by its main designers: Lange's 1936-38 competitive-socialism model, Nove's feasible socialism, Roemer's coupon socialism and Bardhan and Roemer's bank-centric model, Miller's cooperative market socialism, and above all Schweickart's Economic Democracy, with Mill as forerunner and Yugoslav workers' self-management (1950 Basic Law, Tito) as its main historical experiment. Where the state-owned (Lange, Roemer, Nove) and cooperative (Mill, Schweickart, Yugoslav) strands differ, answers are 0 or low. China's and Vietnam's socialist market economies and Proudhonian mutualism are excluded; outside economics most answers are low-confidence inferences.

notes: Strands differ mainly on who holds firms (state or public agencies in Lange, Roemer and Nove; workers in Mill, Schweickart and Yugoslavia) and on interest, which Schweickart would largely abolish but other designs keep. Yugoslav self-management operated under one-party rule, while the modern theorists presuppose multiparty democracy; the profile follows the modern theorists on political questions. Lange later moved toward a mixed public-private economy. Primary books by Lange, Nove, Roemer and Miller could not be opened online, so their positions are cited through scholarly reviews and summaries. Later pass 2026-11-13 (queued for misapplied family approach): answers now rest on the strand's own statements, chiefly Schweickart's 2015 outline of Economic Democracy (s16, answering a questionnaire on economy, society, environment, polity, trade and transition) with Mill and the scholarship; answers that rested only on what adherents or the model's silence suggested, or on Wikipedia, were nulled with the old versions kept in reviewHistory. Schweickart's 1992 article (s1) and the Mises review of Roemer (s10) could not be re-opened (host gone; 403), so no current answer cites them. Themes searched: ownership, markets and planning, investment, labour and unions, welfare, trade, environment, liberty, democracy and transition; foreign policy, religion, gender, culture and law-and-order are not addressed by the defining sources (Schweickart says his work does not address foreign policy).
